beats.vo: Every day you tap glass over and over. How does a flat sheet know where your finger is?
Your body conducts electricity. A phone screen keeps an electric field across its surface, and it notices when a finger disturbs that field.

lines: The screen keeps an *electric field* across its glass.

source.label: Wikipedia, Touchscreen (capacitive and resistive sections), simplified

beats.title: The sensing grid (simplified)
beats.vo: Under the glass is a conductive layer read through a grid of sensing lines. A finger distorts the field near its tip. The controller finds where the change is biggest.

labels: Sensing lines read the field across the glass
A finger distorts the field where it touches
The controller finds the biggest change

source.label: Wikipedia, Touchscreen (capacitive and resistive sections), simplified

beats.title: From tap to location
beats.vo: First the screen holds a steady field. Second, your finger distorts it where you touch. Third, the controller compares the readings and picks the spot that changed most.

steps.title: Field
steps.text: The screen holds a steady electric field

steps.title: Touch
steps.text: Your finger distorts it where you touch

steps.title: Locate
steps.text: The controller finds the biggest change

beats.title: Capacitive vs resistive

source.label: Wikipedia, Touchscreen (capacitive and resistive sections), simplified

beats.vo: Older resistive screens work when two layers are pressed together. Capacitive screens sense a finger's effect on an electric field instead.

left.label: Capacitive
left.note: Senses a finger's effect on an electric field.

right.label: Resistive
right.note: Two layers must be pressed together.

beats.vo: So the glass is not feeling you. It is measuring how you change its field.

data.takeaway: The glass isn't *feeling* you. It's *measuring* a change.
